title: Anthropic Outgrew Git — So It Built Its Own
summary: Anthropic's code merges jumped twelvefold in four months, to more than thirty thousand a day — and Git, built for humans who sometimes go offline, broke under agents that never disconnect. So it built Scion, its own source control system, run by seven engineers. Plus: buying the Google dip after Alphabet's twelve-percent fall, and the dad who cancelled ChatGPT.
bodyMarkdown:
## Anthropic Outgrew Git — So It Built Its Own

Coding is no longer the bottleneck at Anthropic. That is the company’s own diagnosis, and it is worth sitting with, because it inverts the story of the last three years. For a decade, the scarce resource in software was writing code. Now Claude agents write it faster than the systems around them can absorb it — and the thing that breaks first is not the model, but the plumbing built for humans: source control, builds, and continuous integration.

The numbers make the point concrete. In May 2026, Anthropic merged an average of around two thousand five hundred code changes a day. By September, it was merging more than thirty thousand a day — a twelvefold increase in four months. Each of its roughly three thousand staff typically runs ten to fifteen Claude agents in parallel, so the company’s coding output resembles a firm with thirty-five thousand to seventy thousand engineers. Its working copy alone is twenty-five gigabytes, and its continuous integration system performs twenty-five million Git checkouts a day. Git, designed for developers who sometimes go offline and sync later, was never built for clients that are always online, always pushing, at this volume. Anthropic ran hundreds of Git mirrors and still hit a wall: once the repository outgrew the mirrors’ disk capacity, it could no longer scale the repository at all.

So Anthropic built Scion, its own source control system, and Antique, a new code review and code management platform to replace what it lost by leaving GitHub. The design is deliberately simple: server nodes hold the whole repository, changesets live in Google Spanner, and large files live in Google Cloud Storage. It is written in Rust; Antique’s backend is Go with a React frontend. Every component can autoscale, though it has not needed to yet — the data is content-addressed and never changes once stored, so caching tiers do most of the work. One hundred percent of the monorepo has moved off Git, a migration the team says Claude itself was instrumental in completing: get to roughly ninety-nine percent coverage, force the cutover, and let Claude fix whatever actually mattered.

There is a sting in the tail. The creator of Mononoke, an open-source high-throughput version control server, accused Anthropic of ripping off Mononoke’s data model — and Anthropic added a small attribution only after the public complaint. Open source lets you build on others’ work; the complaint is not about permission but about credit. It is a reminder that even infrastructure stories are reputation stories, and Anthropic’s decision not to open-source Scion — “mostly bandwidth,” the team says, with a small team and fast-changing code — sits awkwardly next to Meta’s open-sourcing of Sapling, its own Git replacement.

Orosz’s own hunch is the useful corrective: very few companies will go through the trouble of building another source control system, and most teams do not need to leave Git. The real question is which human-scale assumptions break next. Google is already preparing for ten times more code shipped; a new batch of vendors — Entire, founded by GitHub’s last chief executive Thomas Dohmke, Cursor Origin, and Code Storage — is positioning itself as Git-compatible version control built for AI scale. The bottleneck moved once, from writing code to absorbing it. It will move again, to review, to testing, to deployment. Every team running agents at scale should be asking which of its own pipes was sized for humans, and what happens when the machines fill it twelve times over.

- Agent throughput breaks human-scale infrastructure first: source control, builds, and CI, not model quality.

- Centralised, always-online version control beats Git’s offline assumptions once agents never disconnect.

- A seven-person team can run planetary-scale plumbing if the data model is simple and content-addressed.

- Credit matters as much as code: Anthropic’s attribution arrived only after a public complaint.

Source: The Pragmatic Engineer, “The Pulse: Anthropic builds its own source control system” →

- Anthropic outgrew Git — thirty thousand merges a day forced a new source control system.

- Buying the Google dip — a save on loading up on Alphabet after a twelve-percent fall.

- From the Substacks — the Pragmatic Engineer on infrastructure built for human scale.

When machines do the work, the constraints move. Code got cheap, so the pipes broke; a stock fell, so the dip got bought. In both cases the interesting question is not the first-order event but what it breaks, or opens, next.

## Buying the Google Dip, and the Dad Who Cancelled ChatGPT

Pieter Levels’ post is short, and it captures a market mood in two beats. First, the trade: Google is, in his words, “down bad for no apparent reason,” so he has been loading up on Alphabet stock, which he considers very cheap at these levels. Second, the anecdote: on a video call, his dad told him he had cancelled ChatGPT — the kind of small, personal data point that says more about consumer AI habits than any survey.

The context makes the trade legible. Alphabet fell roughly twelve and a half percent on Thursday, 29 October, after missing third-quarter revenue and earnings expectations: search advertising growth slowed even as cloud revenue more than doubled, while capital spending on AI infrastructure surged. The stock had closed near three hundred and twenty-two dollars and fell to around two hundred and eighty-two. Yesterday’s edition covered the quarter itself; this is the other side of that print — the moment a bad earnings reaction becomes somebody else’s buying opportunity.

Read the two beats together and they pull in opposite directions, which is what makes the post worth saving. The dip-buyer sees a cheap Alphabet; the dad cancelling ChatGPT is a reminder that consumer subscriptions are fickle and that the AI race is still being fought one household at a time. Neither beat settles the question. But for anyone building AI products, the dad is the more useful signal: distribution is not just about model quality, it is about who stays subscribed when the novelty fades.

Source: Pieter Levels on X →
audioTranscript:
Arjun: Good morning. This is The Unread Pile, and today we have a story that flips the last three years of AI on its head. For a long time, the hard part of software was writing the code. Now, at least inside Anthropic, writing the code is the easy part, and something else is breaking instead.

Priya: That is the lead story today, and it comes from Gergely Orosz at The Pragmatic Engineer, who has been talking to the team behind it. Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has built its own source control system. It walked away from Git, the tool almost every developer on earth uses to track code changes. And the reason is a number that is hard to believe until you hear it twice.

Arjun: In May of this year, Anthropic merged an average of about two thousand five hundred code changes every single day. By September, just four months later, that number was more than thirty thousand a day. That is a twelvefold increase in one summer. And the company says it does not expect the growth to slow down, because every bottleneck it removes just leads to even more code being produced.

Priya: So let us slow down and explain the mechanism, because the mechanism is the whole story. Anthropic has roughly three thousand staff. But each of those people typically runs ten to fifteen Claude agents in parallel, all writing code, all the time. So the company's actual coding output looks like a company with thirty-five thousand to seventy thousand engineers. That is the size of Meta or Google, in terms of sheer output, from a company a fraction of that size.

Arjun: And all of that code has to go somewhere. Anthropic keeps its code in one giant shared repository, a monorepo, and the working copy of that repository alone is twenty-five gigabytes. Every one of those thirty thousand daily changes triggers tests, and the testing system performs twenty-five million Git checkouts every single day. Twenty-five million. Git was designed in a different era, for human developers who sometimes worked offline on a laptop and synced up later. It assumes clients disconnect. At Anthropic, the clients never disconnect. They are always online, always pushing.

Priya: That mismatch is what broke. Git scales by running mirrors, copies of the repository spread across many servers. Anthropic was running hundreds of mirrors, and it still hit a wall, because once the repository grew bigger than the mirrors' disk capacity, there was simply no way to scale it further. You cannot mirror your way out of a repository that outgrows the mirrors themselves.

Arjun: So Anthropic built Scion. That is the internal name for its new source control system. And because leaving Git also meant losing GitHub's code review tools, it had to build a second system too, called Antique, for code review and code management. The design of Scion is deliberately simple, which is part of what makes it interesting. Server nodes hold the whole repository. The actual changes are stored in Google Spanner, Google's globally distributed database. Large files live in Google Cloud Storage. The whole thing is written in Rust, and Antique's backend is written in Go with a React frontend.

Priya: And here is the detail that stopped me. The entire system, Scion plus Antique plus code search and merge queues, is built and maintained by seven engineers. Seven people. Four on the core Scion server and client, three split across code search, merge queues, and the rest. That is possible because the data model is simple and content-addressed, meaning once a piece of data is stored it never changes, so caching does most of the heavy lifting. The team says every component can autoscale, but so far it has not even needed to, even as merge volume grew more than tenfold this year.

Arjun: The migration itself is also a story about AI eating its own cooking. One hundred percent of Anthropic's monorepo is now off Git. The team describes the approach as getting to roughly ninety-nine percent coverage and then forcing the cutover, with Claude itself helping to fix whatever actually mattered afterwards. That is a very confident way to migrate the most critical system a software company owns, and it only works if you trust the tool that much.

Priya: Now, there is a sting in the tail, and it matters. The creator of Mononoke, an open-source system built to handle huge numbers of commits, publicly accused Anthropic of copying Mononoke's data model, and said the resemblance went far deeper than one shared idea. Anthropic added a small attribution only after that public complaint. Now, to be clear, open source software is meant to be built upon. That is the whole point of it. The complaint here is not about permission, it is about credit. And it sits awkwardly next to Anthropic's decision not to open-source Scion at all. The team says that is mostly about bandwidth, a small team with fast-changing code. But Meta open-sourced Sapling, its own Git replacement, under similar circumstances. Credit is cheap. Withholding it is a choice, and people notice.

Arjun: Gergely's own take is the useful corrective for the rest of us. Very few companies will go through the trouble of building their own source control system, and most teams do not need to leave Git. His question is better: which of your systems were designed for human scale, and what happens when agents fill them twelve times over? Google, he reports, is already preparing for ten times more code being shipped. And a new batch of vendors is appearing to serve exactly this gap: Entire, founded by GitHub's last chief executive Thomas Dohmke, Cursor Origin, and Code Storage. All of them pitch themselves as Git-compatible version control built for AI scale.

Priya: This is where I want to connect it to you, the listener, especially if you build products. If you run a team that uses coding agents, your bottleneck has already moved, or it is about to. First it was writing code. Then it was reviewing code, which is why people talk about zombie code reviews, where the volume of agent-written changes is so high that people approve without reading. Next it will be testing, deployment, and the review queue itself. The lesson of Scion is not that you should build your own version control. It is that you should go and look at your own pipes, and ask which one was sized for humans, because the agents will find it before you do.

Arjun: Let us go one level deeper on the design, because the design choices are where the general lesson lives. Git's deepest assumption is that a developer works offline and syncs later. That assumption shaped everything: how much data a checkout transfers, how branches merge, how mirrors replicate. At Anthropic, that assumption is simply false. The agents are always connected to the corporate network. So Scion drops the offline machinery entirely. Changesets live in Spanner with multi-region replication, more replicas than the default, because losing code is unacceptable even at the cost of slower writes. On top of replication there are full backups, soft deletes on the blob storage, and point-in-time recovery, so a bad write can be undone. When your clients never disconnect, you can trade away all the machinery built for disconnection, and get speed back in return.

Priya: That same logic explains the precedents. Google ran into this wall years ago. Git did not even exist when Google was founded, so the company used Perforce, and around twenty eleven it built its own system, Piper, when Perforce stopped scaling. Meta went from Mercurial to Sapling, its own client-server system, for the same reason: public tools could not handle a monorepo of that size. In both cases the company did not set out to reinvent version control for fun. It did so because its repository had outgrown the tools that existed, and the alternative, breaking up the monorepo and losing engineering speed, was worse. Anthropic is now the third company to walk this path, except it got there far faster, because agents compressed a decade of growth into four months.

Arjun: And Anthropic's own message to everyone else is refreshingly honest: most teams do not need to leave Git. What Git could use, in their view, is better support for changesets, for derived data, and for the checkout protocol, the exact places where agent scale hurts most. That is a useful framing for a product or engineering leader. You do not need to rebuild the pipe. You need to know which joints in the pipe are under strain. If your team runs ten agents per engineer, your review queue, your test suite, and your deploy pipeline are all living on borrowed time, even if Git itself holds up fine.

Priya: Which brings us back to the question Gergely ends on, and it is the question I would leave you with. How many companies will see Git break the way it broke at Anthropic, and when it does, how many will find that Git's mirroring is inadequate for their needs? The answer will not be everyone. But the companies that feel it first will be the ones whose agents are working hardest. That is a strange new leading indicator: your infrastructure breaks in proportion to how successfully you adopted AI.

Arjun: And there is a second, smaller story in today's pile that rhymes with the first one in an unexpected way. Pieter Levels, the independent founder behind Nomad List and Remote OK, posted that Google stock is down badly for no apparent reason, so he has been loading up on Alphabet shares, which he considers very cheap. And then he adds a personal detail: on a video call, his dad told him he had cancelled ChatGPT.

Priya: The market context makes the trade legible. Alphabet fell roughly twelve and a half percent on Thursday, after missing its third-quarter revenue and earnings expectations. Search advertising growth slowed, even as cloud revenue more than doubled, and spending on AI infrastructure surged. The shares had closed near three hundred and twenty-two dollars, and fell to around two hundred and eighty-two dollars. Yesterday's edition covered the quarter itself. This is the other side of that print: the moment a bad earnings reaction becomes somebody else's buying opportunity.

Arjun: What I like about the post is that its two halves pull in opposite directions. The dip buyer sees a cheap Alphabet, a company with enormous cash flow, a cloud business growing fast, and a Gemini app with a billion users. The dad cancelling ChatGPT is the opposite signal, a reminder that consumer subscriptions are fickle, that novelty fades, and that the AI race is still being fought one household at a time. Both things can be true at once. A stock can be cheap and a product can be losing casual users.

Priya: And for anyone building AI products, the dad is the more useful signal of the two. Distribution is not only about model quality. It is about who stays subscribed when the novelty fades, and why. The companies that win the consumer AI race will not just be the ones with the best model on a benchmark. They will be the ones whose product survives the moment a user asks, out loud, whether they still need it.

Arjun: That is really the through-line of today's edition. When machines do the work, the constraints move somewhere you were not looking. Code got cheap, so the plumbing broke. A stock fell, so the dip got bought, while a dad somewhere quietly cancelled a subscription. In both cases, the interesting question is never just the first-order event. It is what breaks next, and what opens up next.

Priya: That is The Unread Pile for Friday, the thirtieth of October. The full paper, with the charts and the diagrams, is on the website, along with the originals for everything we discussed. We will be back tomorrow morning with the next edition. Until then, go and check your own pipes. They were probably sized for humans too.
